summary: Describes the registry system for distributing globally unique Internet address space and the rules governing it. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7020.

eli5.summary: This was the rulebook for who hands out internet addresses and how. It is out of date now.

questions: how were ip addresses allocated by registries
how were ip addresses allocated in 1996
what is the difference between allocation and assignment
why were ip address assignments treated as loans
subtitle: The 1996 rulebook for how address registries handed out IPv4 space, now replaced.

tldr.problem: IPv4 address space was limited and routers could only cope with so many routes, so address space had to be handed out fairly, in a way that kept routing manageable, and with public records.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes a hierarchy of registries (IANA, regional registries, local registries) and the rules they apply: allocation to ISPs in CIDR blocks, assignment to organizations by demonstrated need, and operating guidelines.
tldr.outcome: It is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7020, so it describes past practice and not current policy.

today: RFC 2050 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 7020, so it records the registry rules of 1996 and is not current policy. It replaced RFC 1466.

sections.title: Goals and the Registry Hierarchy
sections.content:
RFC 2050 is a Best Current Practice that replaces RFC 1466. Its IESG Note says approval means the IESG believes the text accurately represents current practice of the address registries, and does not constitute endorsement of the policy.

Address space is distributed by three goals. Conservation means fair distribution by operational need and no stockpiling. Routability means hierarchical distribution that lets routing scale, though routability is not guaranteed with IPv4 addresses. Registration means a public registry of allocations and assignments, for uniqueness and troubleshooting. Conservation and Routability often conflict.

The Internet Registry hierarchy runs from the top down: IANA, which has authority over all Internet number spaces; regional registries, which at the time were InterNIC (North America), RIPE NCC (Europe) and AP-NIC (Asia Pacific); and local registries, established under the regional registry and IANA, usually of national scope.
sections.eli5: The goals are to share fairly, to keep the maps simple, and to keep a public list of who has what. Three levels of registry hand out the addresses.

sections.title: Allocation to Internet Service Providers
sections.content:
The document distinguishes allocation (regional registries give blocks to ISPs, who assign to customers) from assignment. ISPs that exchange routing information at multiple locations without default routing may ask a regional registry directly. To support hierarchical addressing with CIDR, other ISPs should ask their upstream provider. Direct requests are for ISPs likely to be routable that are connected to a major routing exchange or are multi-homed.

The guidelines include these points:

  • Treat assignments as loans. When a customer leaves, it should return the addresses and renumber into the new provider's space, with enough time allowed.
  • Registries issue space on CIDR bit boundaries and expect efficient use, with documented justification for each assignment.
  • Allocation uses a slow start: new ISPs get a minimal amount, and later allocations give enough space for three months.
  • Requests based on classful assumptions need detailed justification, and static addresses for dial-up users are strongly discouraged.

Assignment information must be submitted to the regional registry immediately, and no further CIDR blocks are allocated until approximately 80% of reassignment information has been submitted.
sections.eli5: Big providers get big blocks and lend small pieces to customers. If a customer moves, the borrowed addresses go back. New providers start small and can ask for more once they show they used the first batch well.

sections.title: Assignment to Organizations
sections.content:
An assignment delegates authority over a block of addresses to an end enterprise that uses them internally only. Regional registry services should be limited to organizations that will never connect to the Internet but need unique addresses (and should consider RFC 1918 space first), that are multi-homed with no favored connection, or that need a very large block, with a prefix of /18 or shorter. Everyone else should ask their ISP.

The basic criteria are a 25% immediate utilization rate and 50% within 1 year, used as a guideline with documented confidence. Organizations with fewer than 128 hosts are not issued addresses directly from the registries, and a prefix longer than /24 may be issued only with documentation from a recognized ISP that it will accept the long prefix into the global routing system.

Registries examine networking plans (subnetting, topology, routing), previous assignment history, deployment plans and organization information. Addresses remain valid while the criteria continue to be met, and IANA can invalidate assignments once the need no longer exists.
sections.eli5: To get addresses directly, an organization must show it needs a lot of them and will really use them. Smaller groups ask their internet provider instead.

sections.title: Operational Guidelines for Registries
sections.content:
Regional registries may charge fees related to the cost of their services. Sub-registries must follow their regional registry's guidelines and make sure their customers do. Assignments are made by prefix length, not by class, so an organization that would have received a Class B now receives a /16.

Requests are subject to audit, and an assignment based on false information may be invalidated. Registries must treat information marked sensitive as confidential. Transfers of addresses between parties must be approved by the regional registries, and the receiver must meet the same criteria as a new requester.

Because of routing system limits, major transit providers may limit CIDR prefix sizes or filter non-aggregated routes. Addresses obtained directly from a regional registry (provider-independent, or portable) are therefore not guaranteed to be routable.

Regional registries maintain IN-ADDR.ARPA records for blocks issued directly to ISPs and for CIDR blocks of less than /16, while local registries and ISPs with a prefix of /16 or shorter maintain records for their customers. An organization that disagrees with an assignment decision may appeal to the parent registry, and finally to IANA.
sections.eli5: The registries may charge a fee, check that requests are honest, keep private details private, and let people appeal if they think a decision was unfair.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. Its main concern with trust is practical: requests are subject to audit and may be invalidated if based on false information.
sections.eli5: The rulebook does not talk about security, but it does let registries check that people are telling the truth.

viz.caption: THE INTERNET REGISTRY HIERARCHY IN RFC 2050

layers.label: IANA
layers.detail: Authority over all Internet number spaces; allocates to regional IRs

layers.label: Regional IRs
layers.detail: InterNIC, RIPE NCC and AP-NIC at the time; continental service areas

layers.label: Local IRs
layers.detail: Established under a regional IR and IANA; usually national scope
